messages.author: c67f07c7216b6f65
messages.subject: Is it possible to identify non-converged ADVI runs in rstan?
parts:
Hi all!

Thank you very much for the work you are putting into stan, it is really providing me with some powerful tools.

I am currently doing some Monte Carlo simulations of a model estimated with ADVI using rstan. Every now and then, it seems there will be an instance where I get the following: "Informational Message: The maximum number of iterations is reached! The algorithm may not have converged. This variational approximation is not guaranteed to be meaningful." (This message can easily be reproduced by setting the "iter"-option of the vb()-command very low.) 

I would like to identify the cases that produce this message, to inspect the results, and possibly exclude them from the main results. Is there a way to do this? I have looked at the content of the stanfit-object, but have not really been able to find anything useful for assessing the convergence status. Am I missing something? Is there some kind of hack I could do, if there is no readymade method for it?

Best,
Joergen

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possibly to identify non-converged ADVI runs in rstan?
parts:
I don't know about the RStan interface to ADVI. I'd hope you
could somehow get a return code or something that indicated whether
everything converged OK according to internal diagnostics.

The deeper problem is that we don't know how to diagnose what's
going wrong with ADVI and we don't have any developers willing
to work on making it more robust. That's why it's still labeled
as "experimental".

And of course we can't give you any model specific advice given that
you haven't said anything about your model. The only way to make sure
things are working that we know of is to run MCMC and compare results.
You probalby want to at least run multiple random inits for ADVI to
make sure you're converging to the same result.

- Bob

Well, for what it’s worth, ADVI seems to produce excellent results in my simulations. Any improvement in accuracy to be had with NUTS is very limited in my case, and as ADVI gives me estimates in a matter of seconds rather than hours, I think it is incredibly valuable. I really hope you won’t remove it (unless you it is because you have found something better).

Also, in case anyone else encounters the issue I originally posted about: My current, not-so-elegant workaround is to use sink() to capture the outputs, and the check whether it contains the non-convergence warning. Here’s an example:

out.file <- file(“output.Rout", open = "wt")
sink(out.file, append=F)
fit <- vb( … ) # Code to fit mode goes here.
sink()
filename <- “output.Rout"
output <- readChar(filename, file.info(filename)$size)
model.failed <- grepl("may not have converged”, output) # Logical indicating convergence issue.

Best,
Joergen

Andrew and a Master’s student are continuing off Rayleigh’s work on benchmarking ADVI. We (Alp and I) halted work on improving ADVI. The first step is to really understand what is causing the failures—we don’t even know that much. This is difficult theoretically, so instead we’re doing a massive empirical analysis. The hope is that these evaluations will then lead to solid heuristics, similar to the conception of NUTS for adapting hyper parameters and R-hat for diagnosing convergence.

dustin

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possibly to identify non-converged ADVI runs in rstan?
parts:
Having estimated means around the true values, or even better using
the estimating variances to quantify that the estimates mean are close
to the true values, is not near sufficient.  That depends too strongly on
the actual model which could place posterior mass away from the true
values.  In other words, a failure could be due to model problems or
computation problems and even a success could be due to computational
problems canceling its modeling problems.

We need to isolate the computational accuracy from the modeling issues 
and test whether or not we are accurately computing posterior expectations.
This is what cannot be done in situ by ADVI where as we have lots of 
diagnostics and guarantees with HMC.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possibly to identify non-converged ADVI runs in rstan?
parts:
Sure, finding a model configuration consistent with the data can be informative.
Just don’t call it full Bayesian inference, which requires quantifying all of the model 
configurations consistent with the data!

On Jan 24, 2017, at 10:20 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

We did the birthday model 3 years ago.  The model on the cover of the book is a culmination of models, each of which revealed more information and made more sense than what came before.  I think that including the model was a better choice than us waiting 4 years until we could fit it using Nuts.
A

On Jan 24, 2017, at 10:19 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

The birthday approximate analysis was useful because it found a model
configuration that looked okay?  That’s one perspective, and the same
argument for many of the machine learning algorithms that “have good
predictive performance” against various point predictions like cross
validation.  

But all of that is based on finding _a_ good point and not accurately
quantifying the uncertainty inherent to the posterior.  The model can
no longer be separated from the computation, and you cannot identify
from which problems are arising.  Decisions are overconfident and 
fragile because of the lack of accurate uncertainty quantification.  In
general inferences become awkward.  Plus, it’s not fair to compare
that to NUTS and not some approximation where you run a Markov
chain for just a few iterations to get into the typical set.

And really the slow performance of NUTS was demonstrating that the
birthday model was highly non-identified, as we have since better
understood.  Again, this doesn’t affect the point approximations but
does slow down NUTS which is doing everything it can to get accurate
uncertainty quantification.  

If this is the argument for these unvalidated approximations then in
my opinion you have to fundamentally change the way you present
the results.  You have to make it very clear that you are presenting
a good point and not quantifying all of the good points, and not really 
comparing to full Bayesian inference at all.  This is an _extremely_
important step to not mislead users.


On Jan 24, 2017, at 9:41 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

I agree that the fake-data check is not perfect, but it's something.  I was pushing back against Jonah's statement, "in order to trust it you'll have to run NUTS anyway, in which case you might as well just use NUTS."  That's fine, but suppose you have a problem where Nuts is too slow to run.  Then you have to do some approx.  ADVI is one choice.

I should elaborate, though, that fake-data checking on the fitted model is not the only confidence-building tool out there.  Another useful approach is to build up a model step by step and check that the inferences make sense at each step.  Another approach is to evaluate errors using cross-validation.  And another is to run ADVI from multiple starting points and compare the different estimates.

These won't give full confidence in results but, again, it's something.  And I think these steps can help.  Recall that we put the birthday model on the cover of our book, and we didn't fit that with Nuts.  And, for that matter, that model isn't perfect.  But the inference for the imperfect model with the imperfect EP algorithm was still useful.

So I resist over-the-top statements such as, "you might as well just use NUTS." 

A

On Jan 24, 2017, at 9:33 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Having estimated means around the true values, or even better using
the estimating variances to quantify that the estimates mean are close
to the true values, is not near sufficient.  That depends too strongly on
the actual model which could place posterior mass away from the true
values.  In other words, a failure could be due to model problems or
computation problems and even a success could be due to computational
problems canceling its modeling problems.

We need to isolate the computational accuracy from the modeling issues 
and test whether or not we are accurately computing posterior expectations.
This is what cannot be done in situ by ADVI where as we have lots of 
diagnostics and guarantees with HMC.

On Jan 24, 2017, at 9:25 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Jonah's statement is a bit extreme, I think.  Another way to check ADVI is to simulate fake data from some versions of the fitted model and see if ADVI recovers the parameter values.
A


On Jan 24, 2017, at 7:14 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Jorgen,

I'm glad it produces good results for you, but the problem is that you wouldn't know that without comparing to NUTS. So until we have some way of better diagnosing advi runs, in order to trust it you'll have to run NUTS anyway, in which case you might as well just use NUTS. 

Jonah 

On Tue, Jan 24, 2017 at 5:17 PM Jørgen Bølstad <j.boe...@gmail.com> wrote:
Well, for what it’s worth, ADVI seems to produce excellent results in my simulations. Any improvement in accuracy to be had with NUTS is very limited in my case, and as ADVI gives me estimates in a matter of seconds rather than hours, I think it is incredibly valuable. I really hope you won’t remove it (unless you it is because you have found something better).



Also, in case anyone else encounters the issue I originally posted about: My current, not-so-elegant workaround is to use sink() to capture the outputs, and the check whether it contains the non-convergence warning. Here’s an example:



out.file <- file(“output.Rout", open = "wt")

sink(out.file, append=F)

fit <- vb( … ) # Code to fit mode goes here.

sink()

filename <- “output.Rout"

output <- readChar(filename, file.info(filename)$size)

model.failed <- grepl("may not have converged”, output) # Logical indicating convergence issue.



Best,

Joergen





On Jan 24, 2017, at 10:54 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:





On Jan 24, 2017, at 10:02 AM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:



On Monday, January 23, 2017 at 4:21:50 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:



The deeper problem is that we don't know how to diagnose what's

going wrong with ADVI and we don't have any developers willing

to work on making it more robust.  That's why it's still labeled

as "experimental".



Are Alp and Dustin not working on this at all anymore?



Nope.  Their last commits to ADVI were in 2015.



We may just remove ADVI if we can't find anyone to fix it.  I don't

want to leave algorithms in Stan that aren't robust and don't have

good failure diagnostics---it just frustrates our users no matter

how much we try to point out it's "experimental".



- Bob

I think Andrew's making a good point here. Before Stan, I
was writing "machine learning" algorithms for natural language
processing (LDA, L1-penalized logistic regression, conditional random
fields, language models for spell checking, etc.) In almost all of
these cases, simpler models with more data have always outperformed
more complex models predictively in terms of 0/1 loss. We're talking gigabytes
of training data here. I don't see anything wrong with that. We need
to build spell checkers, named-entity finders, classifiers for sites
like Google news, etc.

But Michael also makes a good point that there should be some kind
of discussion of approximation error. Or at least an acknowledgement
that the posterior approximation is of unknown quality. In a lot of
what I've seen in the natural language literature, variational inference
is just being performed for a point estimate.

We didn't run with simulated data, but we ran with data where we
had the HMC fit, and saw that ADVI failed to recover the true posteiror
means within 1 posterior standard deviation in most cases. And the
real problem is that when it fails on real data, we don't know how to diagnose
that. Fitting with data simulated from a model is often insufficient because
the model is misspecified for real data.

We also know that variational inference underestimates posterior uncertainty
by construction, because of the direction of KL divergence minimized. So if
we do simulated data, we should have too low posterior coverage of p-intervals.

I think a lot of machine learning researchers only care about
predictions, which can also be calibrated and evaluated for
sharpness (how narrow the intervals are).

So we can test that calibration. And we can even do it in a believable
way if we have held out data, we can test that calibration on real
predictions.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possibly to identify non-converged ADVI runs in rstan?
parts:
Hi, the short answer to both questions is that I'd like to develop something formal, along the lines of R-hat (for item 1) or my paper with Cook and Rubin (for item 2), but for now the answer is that Jørgen Bølstad (the person who wrote that email) should look at the estimate and see if they're close enough for practical purposes, based on his own goals in fitting the model. Jørgen is his own homunculus.

Yes, though, we should definitely come up with some formulas for this and code them up, and then people can try them out.

I'm fine to use Nuts to calibrate. But that won't work for problems where Nuts is just too slow.

A

> On Jan 25, 2017, at 4:37 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> 1. How do you test for similarity? As in, I have the simulated
> value and I have the posterior mean and marginal posterior standard
> deviation from the estimate, what do I do?
>
> 2. What do you mean by close? Close as in the true values are
> in an appropriate number of posterior intervals?
>
> We want to write code. We can't build a homunculus to replace
> you unless we know what you'd do.
>
> I get that you don't want to use MCMC results to calibrate.
>
> But I don't even understand if you only want to test the
> posterior mean point estimates, or if you also care about
> posterior uncertainty. And I don't see why you wouldn't just
> take the posterior approximation and simulate from that then
> use R-hat. But then you could probably calculate R-hat analytically
> from that since it's multivariate Gaussian.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>

>> I mean 2 things:
>> 1. Running ADVI on the data several times and checking that the resulting estimates are similar. Ultimately I think there should be an R-hat-like test here but I don't have that yet.
>> 2. Fake-data simulation: Choosing reasonable hypothetical values for the hyperparameters of the model, then simulating local parameters and data, then running ADVI and checking to see if the resulting estimate is close, both for the hyperparameters and the true values.
>> A
